claim: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is diagnosed in about 1% of children.
source: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition of impaired social communication and restrictive behaviour, diagnosed in about 1% of children (Lai et al., 2014; Baio et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Lai et al., 2014 and Baio et al., 2018

claim: ASD is associated with extensive heterogeneity of behavioral symptoms and neurobiological endophenotypes.
source: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental condition of impaired social communication and restrictive behaviour, diagnosed in about 1% of children (Lai et al., 2014; Baio et al., 2018), that is associated with extensive heterogeneity of behavioral symptoms and neurobiological endophenotypes (Jacob et al., 2019; Lombardo et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacob et al., 2019 and Lombardo et al., 2019

claim: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has emerged as a promising technology to identify potential biomarkers of functional connectivity (FC) in ASD and other psychiatric disorders.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has emerged as a promising technology to identify potential biomarkers of functional connectivity (FC) in ASD and other psychiatric disorders (Castellanos et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Castellanos et al., 2013

claim: Efforts to characterize the functional brain organization in ASD have so far largely focused on case-control comparisons, thus ignoring the presumed heterogeneity of FC alterations.
source: However, efforts to characterize the functional brain organization in ASD have so far largely focused on case-control comparisons, thus ignoring the presumed heterogeneity of FC alterations (Nunes et al., 2019; Hahamy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nunes et al., 2019 and Hahamy et al., 2015

claim: Data driven cluster analysis has long been proposed as a solution to decompose the heterogeneity of behavioral symptoms in ASD into distinct subtypes.
source: Data driven cluster analysis has long been proposed as a solution to decompose the heterogeneity of behavioral symptoms in ASD into distinct subtypes (Eaves et al., 1994; Beglinger and Smith, 2001)
evidence: Supported by citations to Eaves et al., 1994 and Beglinger and Smith, 2001

claim: Behavioral subtypes in ASD have proven difficult to distinguish in clinical practice.
source: but these subtypes have proven difficult to distinguish in clinical practice (Lord et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Lord et al., 2012

claim: Behavioral subtypes in ASD were recently abandoned in favour of the broader concept of an autism spectrum.
source: but these subtypes have proven difficult to distinguish in clinical practice (Lord et al., 2012) and were recently abandoned in favour of the broader concept of an autism spectrum (American Psychiatric Association. and DSM-5 American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to American Psychiatric Association and DSM-5, 2013

claim: The lack of progress toward reproducible, brain-based biomarkers of ASD has renewed interest in clustering methods to decompose the heterogeneity of brain alterations into distinct subtypes.
source: The lack of progress toward reproducible, brain-based biomarkers of ASD (Lombardo et al., 2019) has renewed interest in clustering methods to decompose the heterogeneity of brain alterations into distinct subtypes that are hypothesized to underlie the multitude of behavioral symptoms.
evidence: Supported by citation to Lombardo et al., 2019

claim: Early work on subcortical volume alterations in ASD distinguished four subtypes but did not find significant differences of behavioral symptoms between them.
source: Early work on subcortical volume alterations in ASD has distinguished four subtypes, but did not find significant differences of behavioral symptoms between them (Hrdlicka et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hrdlicka et al., 2005

claim: A multi-modal analysis distinguished three subtypes of structural brain alterations in ASD and found that core ASD symptoms could be much better predicted from the structural MRI data when separate prediction models were trained on each subtype compared to the full, unstratified dataset.
source: A more recent multi-modal analysis distinguished three subtypes of structural brain alterations in ASD and found that core ASD symptoms could be much better predicted from the structural MRI data when separate prediction models were trained on each subtype compared to the full, unstratified dataset (Hong et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hong et al., 2018

claim: Work on the heterogeneity of FC in individuals with ASD, ADHD, and NTC distinguished three FC subtypes among regions in the default mode network and found that each FC subtype was associated with all three diagnostic groups.
source: Work on the heterogeneity of FC in individuals with ASD, attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), and neurotypical controls (NTC) distinguished three FC subtypes among regions in the default mode network (DMN) and found that each FC subtype was associated with all three diagnostic groups, indicating that these FC subtypes may be shared across diagnostic boundaries (Kernbach et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kernbach et al., 2018

claim: An analysis of whole-brain FC in ASD and NTC individuals distinguished two FC subtypes of diverging within- and between-network connectivity, but showed that the assignment of individuals to these FC subtypes was not associated to their clinical diagnosis.
source: An analysis of whole-brain FC in ASD and NTC individuals distinguished two FC subtypes of diverging within- and between-network connectivity, but similarly showed that the assignment of individuals to these FC subtypes was not associated to their clinical diagnosis (Easson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Easson et al., 2019

claim: The stability of discrete and continuous methods of assigning individuals to subtypes has not been systematically established.
source: Firstly, studies have so far interpreted imaging subtypes both as discrete categories (Hrdlicka et al., 2005; Hong et al., 2018) and a continuous, multifactorial spectrum (Kernbach et al., 2018; Easson et al., 2019). However, the stability of either of these two methods of assigning individuals to subtypes has not been systematically established.
evidence: Inferred from the statement that stability has not been systematically established

claim: Behavioral symptoms in ASD overlap with those of other neurodevelopmental disorders and also extend into the general population.
source: Behavioral symptoms in ASD overlap with those of other neurodevelopmental disorders and also extend into the general population (Constantino and Todd, 2003; Grzadzinski et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Constantino and Todd, 2003 and Grzadzinski et al., 2011

claim: Neurobiological endophenotypes associated with ASD have been shown to exist among individuals with other neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: Similarly, neurobiological endophenotypes associated with ASD have been shown to exist among individuals with other neuropsychiatric disorders (Park et al., 2018; Di Martino et al., 2013; Moreau et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Park et al., 2018, Di Martino et al., 2013, and Moreau et al., 2020

claim: None of the imaging subtypes associated with ASD in the literature have been replicated to date.
source: Thirdly, none of the imaging subtypes associated with ASD in the literature have been replicated to date.
evidence: Direct statement about lack of replication in the literature

claim: The recent failure to replicate promising reports of clinically meaningful neuroimaging subtypes in depression has highlighted the importance of replication for the autism literature.
source: The recent failure to replicate promising reports of clinically meaningful neuroimaging subtypes in depression (Drysdale et al., 2017; Dinga et al., 2019) has highlighted the importance of this limitation for the autism literature.
evidence: Supported by citations to Drysdale et al., 2017 and Dinga et al., 2019

claim: Alterations of FC in different brain networks have been previously linked to different behavioral and cognitive symptoms of ASD.
source: Alterations of FC in different brain networks have been previously linked to different behavioral and cognitive symptoms of ASD (Rudie et al., 2012; Cerliani et al., 2015; Abbott et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rudie et al., 2012, Cerliani et al., 2015, and Abbott et al., 2016

claim: The MIST_20 functional brain parcellation has been shown to perform well in ASD related classification tasks.
source: To probe the connectivity of functional brain networks, we defined FC seed regions with a functional connectivity derived brain parcellation (Urchs et al., 2017) that has been shown to perform well in ASD related classification tasks (Dadi et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dadi et al., 2019

claim: 87 FC subtypes were identified in the discovery dataset across all 18 seed networks.
source: Across all 18 seed networks, we identified 87 FC subtypes in the discovery dataset
evidence: Direct statement of the number of FC subtypes identified

claim: Between 3 and 6 FC subtypes were identified in each seed network, with a median of 5.
source: In each seed network we identified between 3 (medial visual network) and 6 FC subtypes (lateral visual network) that satisfied the criteria (the median number of FC subtypes was 5).
evidence: Direct statement of the range and median number of FC subtypes per network

claim: On average across networks, 97% of the individuals in the discovery dataset were assigned to a FC subtype.
source: On average across networks, 97% of the individuals in the discovery dataset were assigned to a FC subtype
evidence: Direct statement of the percentage of individuals assigned to FC subtypes

claim: No significant linear relationship was found between continuous assignments of individuals to FC subtypes and in-scanner head motion or age for any seed network.
source: Lastly, we found no significant linear relationship between continuous assignments of individuals to FC subtypes and in-scanner head motion, and age for any seed network (Pearson's correlation).
evidence: Statistical test result showing no significant association with head motion or age

claim: The spatial maps of the identified FC subtypes were stable across perturbations in the discovery dataset.
source: We thus showed that the spatial maps of the identified FC subtypes were stable across perturbations in the discovery dataset .
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the stability analysis results

claim: The discrete assignment of an individual to a FC subtype was not stable to perturbations in the discovery dataset.
source: We thus showed that the discrete assignment of an individual to a FC subtype was not stable to perturbations in the discovery dataset.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the low Dice coefficient results

claim: ICC of continuous assignments to FC subtypes increased both as a function of the number of included scan sessions and also as a function of the total amount of available time frames.
source: We found that ICC of continuous assignments to FC subtypes increased both as a function of the number of included scan sessions and also as a function of the total amount of available time frames (Figure 3).
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the controlled analysis and shown in Figure 3

claim: The stability of continuous assignments to FC subtypes ranges from poor to excellent as a function of the amount of available data per individual and whether FC subtypes and continuous assignments are computed on the same data.
source: We thus showed that the stability of continuous assignments to FC subtypes ranges from poor to excellent as a function of the amount of available data per individual and whether FC subtypes and continuous assignments are computed on the same data.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the stability analyses

claim: 11 FC subtypes were identified for which the continuous assignment of individuals were significantly associated with the clinical diagnosis of ASD, after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: We identified 11 FC subtypes for which the continuous assignment of individuals were significantly associated with the clinical diagnosis of ASD, after correction for multiple comparisons
evidence: Direct statement of the number of FC subtypes significantly associated with ASD diagnosis

claim: NTC individuals showed significantly stronger continuous assignments than ASD individuals with 5 of the 11 FC subtypes (negASD FC subtypes).
source: NTC individuals showed significantly stronger continuous assignments than ASD individuals with 5 of the 11 FC subtypes (i.e. the association with ASD diagnosis was negative).
evidence: Direct statement of the number and direction of associations

claim: The negASD FC subtype maps are characterized by above average FC within each seed network, above average FC in overlapping brain regions (particularly within sensorimotor areas, visual areas, and auditory areas), and below average FC in overlapping brain regions (particularly within areas of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and subcortical areas).
source: The negASD FC subtype maps share a number of characteristics, despite originating from different seed networks: they are characterized by above average FC within each seed network (seed network denoted by a bright green outline); they show above average FC in overlapping brain regions, particularly within sensorimotor areas around the central sulcus, visual areas in the occipital cortex, auditory areas along the superior temporal gyri and opercula; and they show below average FC in overlapping brain regions, particularly within areas of the ventromedial prefrontal cortex and subcortical areas involving the basal ganglia and thalamus.
evidence: Description of the spatial patterns observed in the negASD FC subtype maps

claim: ASD individuals showed significantly stronger continuous assignments than NTC individuals with 6 of the 11 FC subtypes (posASD FC subtypes).
source: ASD individuals showed significantly stronger continuous assignments than NTC individuals with 6 of the 11 FC subtypes (i.e. the association with ASD diagnosis was positive).
evidence: Direct statement of the number and direction of associations

claim: The posASD FC subtype maps generally show below average FC within each seed network and an overall pattern of below average FC throughout the brain.
source: The posASD FC subtype maps also share a number of characteristics, despite originating from different seed networks: they generally show below average FC within each seed network and they show an overal pattern of below average FC throughout the brain.
evidence: Description of the spatial patterns observed in the posASD FC subtype maps

claim: Compared to negASD FC subtype maps, posASD FC subtype maps appear more heterogeneous in their profile of FC alteration.
source: Compared to negASD FC subtype maps, posASD FC subtype maps appear more heterogeneous in their profile of FC alteration.
evidence: Comparative observation of the spatial patterns

claim: A subset of the identified FC subtypes naturally captured some inter-individual variation of the clinical ASD diagnosis.
source: We thus showed that a subset of the identified FC subtypes naturally captured some inter-individual variation of the clinical ASD diagnosis.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the association analysis

claim: Three FC subtypes that were negatively associated with ASD in the discovery sample were identified in the subsample with complete brain coverage including the cerebellum.
source: We identified three FC subtypes that were negatively associated with ASD in the discovery sample.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of negASD FC subtypes in the cerebellar analysis

claim: No cerebellar FC subtypes were found to be significantly associated with ASD diagnosis.
source: No cerebellar FC subtypes were found to be significantly associated with ASD diagnosis.
evidence: Direct statement of the lack of significant associations for cerebellar FC subtypes

claim: The spatial topography of the negASD FC subtypes identified in the subsample with full brain coverage (including the cerebellum) was very similar to the shared topography among negASD FC subtypes identified in the main analysis (excluding the cerebellum).
source: In general, the spatial topography of the negASD FC subtypes identified in the subsample with full brain coverage (including the cerebellum) was very similar to the shared topography among negASD FC subtypes identified in the main analysis (excluding the cerebellum).
evidence: Comparative observation of spatial patterns between analyses

claim: The exclusion of the cerebellum in the main analysis did not change the central findings.
source: We thus concluded that the exclusion of the cerebellum in our main analysis did not change our central findings.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the comparison of analyses with and without cerebellum

claim: No significant association was observed between total ADOS scores and continuous assignments to FC subtypes beyond the effect of ASD diagnosis.
source: We did not observe any significant association between total ADOS scores and continuous assignments to FC subtypes beyond the effect of ASD diagnosis.
evidence: Direct statement of the lack of significant associations with ADOS scores

claim: No significant association was observed between total ADOS scores and continuous FC subtype assignments in the subsample of ASD individuals in the discovery dataset.
source: We did not observe any significant association between total ADOS scores and continuous FC subtype assignments in the subsample of ASD individuals in the discovery dataset.
evidence: Direct statement of the lack of significant associations in the ASD-only subsample

claim: The FC subtype associated with SRS scores was also significantly associated with ASD diagnosis and showed the strongest effect size of all posASD FC subtypes (Cohen's d=0.38).
source: This FC subtype was also significantly associated with ASD diagnosis and showed the strongest effect size of all posASD FC subtypes (cohens-d=0.38).
evidence: Direct statement of the association with ASD diagnosis and effect size

claim: The shared spatial pattern of negASD FC subtypes was characterized by overconnectivity with unimodal sensory brain networks, and underconnectivity with the basal ganglia and fronto-parietal network.
source: By dividing all FC subtype maps into the 18 seed networks, we observed that the shared spatial pattern of negASD FC subtypes was characterized by overconnectivity with unimodal sensory brain networks, and underconnectivity with the basal ganglia and fronto-parietal network (green hues, Figure 4c).
evidence: Description of the spatial pattern observed in Figure 4c

claim: The shared spatial pattern of posASD FC subtypes was characterized by pervasive underconnectivity.
source: By contrast, the shared spatial pattern of posASD FC subtypes was characterized by pervasive underconnectivity (red hues, Figure 4c).
evidence: Description of the spatial pattern observed in Figure 4c

claim: negASD and posASD FC subtypes exhibited similarities of FC alteration and continuous assignments, and these similarities were more pronounced for negASD FC subtypes than posASD FC subtypes.
source: We thus showed that negASD and posASD FC subtypes exhibited similarities of FC alteration and continuous assignments, and that these similarities were more pronounced for negASD FC subtypes than posASD FC subtypes.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the spatial and assignment correlation analyses

claim: Seven FC subtypes that originated from primary sensory seed networks in the motor, auditory and visual networks were significantly associated with ASD diagnosis after correcting for whole-brain FC.
source: We found seven FC subtypes that originated from primary sensory seed networks seeds in the motor, auditory and visual networks, (see Figure 6) and were significantly associated with ASD diagnosis.
evidence: Direct statement of the number and origin of FC subtypes after whole-brain FC correction

claim: Three of the FC subtypes corrected for whole-brain FC were negatively associated with ASD (negASD) and showed strong topographic similarity that closely resembled the previously identified profile of negASD FC subtypes not corrected for whole-brain FC.
source: Three of the FC subtypes were negatively associated with ASD (negASD) and showed strong topographic similarity of their FC subtype maps that very closely resembled the previously identified profile of negASD FC subtypes not corrected for whole-brain FC.
evidence: Description of the negASD FC subtypes after whole-brain FC correction

claim: The negASD pattern after correcting for whole-brain FC was characterized by above-average FC in brain regions associated with primary sensory functions such as motor, visual, and auditory regions, and by below average connectivity with medial-prefrontal and subcortical regions.
source: This negASD pattern was characterized by above-average FC in brain regions associated with primary sensory functions such as motor, visual, and auditory regions, and by below average connectivity with medial-prefrontal and subcortical regions.
evidence: Description of the spatial pattern of negASD FC subtypes after whole-brain FC correction

claim: Four FC subtypes corrected for whole-brain FC were positively associated with ASD (posASD) and showed topographic similarity of their FC subtypes maps, in contrast to posASD FC subtypes not corrected for whole-brain FC.
source: The remaining four FC subtypes were positively associated with ASD (posASD) and, in contrast to posASD FC subtypes not corrected for whole-brain FC, showed topographic similarity of their FC subtypes maps.
evidence: Description of the posASD FC subtypes after whole-brain FC correction

claim: The posASD pattern after correcting for whole-brain FC was the inverse of the negASD pattern, characterized by below average FC in sensory brain areas and above average FC in subcortical and ventromedial regions, and in the precuneus.
source: This posASD pattern was the inverse of the negASD pattern, and thus characterized by below average FC in sensory brain areas and above average FC in subcortical and ventromedial regions, and in the precuneus.
evidence: Description of the spatial pattern of posASD FC subtypes after whole-brain FC correction

claim: All effects of association with diagnosis in the replication sample had the same direction as in the discovery sample.
source: We found that all effects of association with diagnosis in the replication sample had the same direction as in the discovery sample.
evidence: Direct statement of the replication results

claim: The magnitude of the estimated effects in the replication sample was on average 63% of those estimated in the discovery sample.
source: The magnitude of the estimated effects in the replication sample was on average 63% of those estimated in the discovery sample
evidence: Direct statement of the relative magnitude of replication effects

claim: Nine out of eleven effect size estimates in the replication sample fell within the 90% confidence intervals of the effect size estimates in the discovery sample.
source: and nine out of eleven effect size estimates fell within the 90% confidence intervals of the effect size estimates in the discovery sample.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of replicated effects within confidence intervals

claim: The association between FC subtypes and ASD diagnosis observed on the discovery dataset was moderately replicable in the independent replication dataset.
source: We thus showed that the association between FC subtypes and ASD diagnosis observed on the discovery dataset was moderately replicable in the independent replication dataset.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the replication analysis

claim: Data driven FC subtypes are moderately reliable on currently available datasets.
source: Our results suggest that data driven FC subtypes are moderately reliable on currently available datasets
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the stability and replication analyses

claim: Functional connectivity subtypes show a weak to moderate association with the clinical diagnosis of ASD, and these associations generalize to independent replication data.
source: Our results suggest that data driven FC subtypes are moderately reliable on currently available datasets and show a weak to moderate association with the clinical diagnosis of ASD, that generalizes to independent replication data.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the association and replication analyses

claim: The findings are consistent with previous studies that reported stable imaging subtypes in ASD.
source: This observation fits with previous studies that reported stable imaging subtypes in ASD (Hong et al., 2018; Easson et al., 2019; Tang et al., 2020).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature supported by citations

claim: The findings are consistent with the study of Dinga et al., 2019 that could not replicate discrete subtypes originally described in depressed patients.
source: Our findings are consistent with the study of Dinga et al., 2019 that could not replicate discrete subtypes originally described in depressed patients (Drysdale et al., 2017) using an independent dataset.
evidence: Comparison with previous literature supported by citations

claim: The robustness of discrete subtype assignments has been more comprehensively investigated for symptom based subtypes in the wider ASD literature.
source: In the wider ASD literature, the robustness of discrete subtype assignments has been more comprehensively investigated for symptom based subtypes.
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature

claim: Several symptom based subtypes of autism have been proposed but the distinction between these subtypes was not found to be well supported by replication attempts.
source: Several symptom based subtypes of autism have been proposed in attempts to provide more homogeneous diagnostic criteria. However, the distinction between these subtypes was also not found to be well supported by replication attempts
evidence: Statement about the history of symptom-based subtypes in ASD

claim: The field has merged sub-diagnoses of autism under the label of autism spectrum disorder.
source: which has led the field to merge sub-diagnoses of autism under the label of autism spectrum disorder (Lord et al., 2012; Volkmar and McPartland, 2014).
evidence: Statement about diagnostic practice supported by citations

claim: The results support the view that subtypes should be conceptualized as latent dimensions that can be expressed to varying degrees in each individual.
source: An emerging body of literature therefore conceptualizes subtypes as latent dimensions that can be expressed to varying degrees in each individual (Kernbach et al., 2018; Tang et al., 2020; Easson et al., 2019). Our own results support this view
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the results and comparison with literature

claim: Unlike discrete assignments to FC subtypes, continuous measures of an individuals' similarity with each FC subtype are moderately robust and can be very robust when more data is available per individual.
source: we find that, unlike discrete assignments to FC subtypes, continuous measures of an individuals' similarity with each FC subtype are moderately robust and can be very robust when more data is available per individual to compute the continuous assignment.
evidence: Summary conclusion drawn from the stability analyses

claim: The ICC of continuous assignments to FC subtypes computed on separate data was low but consistent with previous reports of the robustness of single session seed based FC measures.
source: The ICC of continuous assignments to FC subtypes computed on separate data was low but consistent with previous reports of the robustness of single session seed based FC measures (Shehzad et al., 2009; Birn et al., 2013; Noble et al., 2019).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature supported by citations

claim: The high to very high stability measures for continuous assignments computed from multiple scan sessions are in line with the well-established link between scan length and FC reliability.
source: When the continuous assignments to FC subtypes were computed based on the average FC of multiple scan sessions per individual, we found high to very high stability measures that were in line with the well-established link between scan length and FC reliability (Gordon et al., 2017).
evidence: Comparison with established knowledge supported by citation

claim: Both the number of averaged scan sessions and the total number of included time points across sessions contribute to the observed increase of ICC, although scan duration leads to markedly higher gains in stability.
source: We further clarified this relationship by showing that both the number of averaged scan sessions and also the total number of included time points across sessions contribute to the observed increase of ICC, although scan duration leads to markedly higher gains in stability.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the controlled analysis of session number and time points

claim: The generalizability of the associations between continuous assignments and clinical ASD diagnosis may increase if longer or repeated scan sessions were available for the replication sample.
source: The generalizability of the associations between continuous assignments and clinical ASD diagnosis may thus increase if longer or repeated scan sessions were available for the replication sample.
evidence: Speculation based on the observed relationship between data amount and stability

claim: The effect sizes of associations between FC subtypes and ASD diagnosis are comparable to those reported by other imaging based subtypes in ASD.
source: Our effect sizes are comparable to those reported by other imaging based subtypes in ASD, which have all estimated association with diagnosis in their discovery sample (i.e. have not been replicated on independent data).
evidence: Comparison with previous literature

claim: The magnitude of the association between data driven FC subtypes and clinical diagnosis is comparable to what has been previously reported by other imaging based subtypes analyses of ASD.
source: The magnitude of the association between data driven FC subtypes and clinical diagnosis in our analyses is therefore comparable to what has been previously reported by other imaging based subtypes analyses of ASD.
evidence: Comparison with previous literature

claim: Weak-to-moderate associations between data driven FC subtypes and clinical diagnosis seem robust to the employed subtyping method, at least in the currently limited number of published studies.
source: Weak-to-moderate associations between data driven FC subtypes and clinical diagnosis thus seem robust to the employed subtyping method, at least in the currently limited number of published studies.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from comparison with literature

claim: A previous study on FC derived imaging subtypes found that dividing individuals into two subtypes allowed for multivariate relationships between FC, ADOS, and SRS scores to be revealed.
source: A second study on FC derived imaging subtypes in a mixed sample of both ASD and NTC individuals (Easson et al., 2019) found that two whole-brain imaging subtypes best approximated the data, and that dividing individuals into these two subtypes allowed for multivariate relationships between FC, ADOS, and SRS scores (among others) to be revealed.
evidence: Description of previous study results supported by citation

claim: The study investigated a simple linear relationship between FC subtype assignments and ASD severity measures, whereas previous studies used subtyping findings to stratify their sample before conducting a multivariate model fit using all brain features.
source: One explanation for the different findings is that we investigated a simple linear relationship between FC subtype assignments and ASD severity measures, whereas previous studies used subtyping findings to stratify their sample before conducting a multivariate model fit using all brain features.
evidence: Explanation for the difference in findings compared to previous studies

claim: It is possible that combining many FC subtype assignment scores in a multivariate prediction model would lead to stronger prediction of ASD severity.
source: It is possible that similarly combining many FC subtype assignment scores in a multivariate prediction model would lead to stronger prediction of ASD severity.
evidence: Speculation about potential alternative analysis approach

claim: Very few imaging based subtype analyses have been replicated on independent data, and to the authors' knowledge none have so far been replicated successfully.
source: Very few imaging based subtype analyses have been replicated on independent data, and to our knowledge none have so far been replicated successfully (Dinga et al., 2019).
evidence: Statement about the state of the literature supported by citation

claim: The replication of the results on independent data establishes a novel benchmark of reliability for imaging based subtype analyses in ASD.
source: The replication of our results on independent data therefore establishes a novel benchmark of reliability for imaging based subtype analyses in ASD.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the replication results and comparison with literature

claim: The reduction of effect sizes on the replication data is expected as it reflects the inherent bias of significance testing to select larger effects.
source: This reduction of effect sizes on the replication data is expected as it reflects the inherent bias of significance testing to select larger effects and further underlines the importance of reporting original findings together with independent replications for an unbiased estimate (Vul and Pashler, 2012).
evidence: Explanation of the reduction in effect sizes supported by citation

claim: The hypothesis that FC subtypes linked to different seed networks might be linked to distinct behavioral ASD symptom profiles was not supported by the findings.
source: In our analyses, we hypothesized that FC subtypes linked to different seed networks might be linked to distinct behavioral ASD symptom profiles. This hypothesis was not supported by our findings.
evidence: Direct statement that the hypothesis was not supported

claim: The converging topography among the identified ASD-related FC subtypes suggests that all FC subtypes capture different views of a single underlying FC profile characterized by a distinction between unimodal and transmodal FC.
source: The converging topography among the identified ASD-related FC subtypes rather suggests that all FC subtypes capture different views of a single underlying FC profile characterized by a distinction between unimodal and transmodal FC, with negASD and posASD FC subtypes situated at opposite ends of a shared dimension.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the observed spatial patterns

claim: When correcting for individual differences in average global FC, posASD FC subtypes showed a topography of FC alteration opposite of that shown by negASD FC subtypes.
source: When we corrected for individual differences in average global FC, we identified posASD FC subtypes that showed a topography of FC alteration opposite of that shown by negASD FC subtypes: below average FC within and between unimodal brain networks, and above average FC with transmodal regions.
evidence: Description of the results after correcting for global FC

claim: A supplemental principal component analysis confirmed that across all 18 seed networks, the components explaining the largest amount of FC variance captured whole-brain shifts in FC.
source: We confirmed this observation by a supplemental principal component analysis (Appendix 3—figure 1). Across all 18 seed networks, the components explaining the largest amount of FC variance captured whole-brain shifts in FC.
evidence: Reference to supplemental analysis shown in Appendix 3—figure 1

claim: The spatial pattern from the principal component analysis is strikingly similar to the case-control Holiga map.
source: The spatial pattern is strikingly similar to the case-control Holiga map (Figure 7).
evidence: Comparison with previous study shown in Figure 7

claim: The specific pattern of connectivity differences is in line with a view of the connectome as organized along major gradients, the most dominant of which parses the brain from sensori-to-associative.
source: The specific pattern of connectivity differences is also very much in line with a view of the connectome as organized along major gradients, the most dominant of which parses the brain from sensori-to-associative.
evidence: Interpretation of the results in the context of gradient theory

claim: The results can be interpreted as a compression of the gradient (less segregation) in ASD, which is a similar conclusion to a recent gradient-based analysis in ASD.
source: Our results here can then be interpreted as a compression of the gradient (less segregation) in ASD, which is a similar conclusion to a recent gradient-based analysis in ASD, also in ABIDE (Hong et al., 2019a).
evidence: Interpretation of the results and comparison with previous study supported by citation

claim: The observation of gradient compression was not an assumption made by the model, but rather a conclusion reached by parsing many seed regions.
source: This observation was not an assumption made by our model, but rather a conclusion reached by parsing many seed regions, and stands opposite to our initial hypothesis.
evidence: Statement about the nature of the finding

claim: If granular and symptom-specific FC subtypes do exist, they are dominated by larger variations in gradients which would need to be taken into account.
source: If granular and symptom-specific FC subtypes do exist, they are dominated by larger variations in gradients which would need to be taken into account.
evidence: Speculation about potential future findings

claim: It is possible that FC subtypes not associated with ASD may carry important, complementary information which would only become apparent in multivariate analysis combining different seeds, or with a larger sample with increased statistical power.
source: It is also possible that FC subtypes not associated with ASD may carry important, complementary information which would only become apparent in multivariate analysis combining different seeds, or with a larger sample with increased statistical power.
evidence: Speculation about potential future findings

claim: The replication of association between FC subtypes and ASD between ABIDE 1 and ABIDE 2 seemed to extend to many subtypes which were not significant after correction for multiple comparisons.
source: The replication of association between FC subtypes and ASD between ABIDE 1 and ABIDE 2 indeed seemed to extend to many subtypes which were not significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Figure 8).
evidence: Observation from Figure 8

claim: The analysis only included male individuals, which is a common problem in the field due to the higher frequency of ASD diagnosis among male individuals.
source: First, our analyses only included male individuals which is a common problem in the field (Khundrakpam et al., 2017; Hong et al., 2019a) due to the higher frequency of ASD diagnosis among male individuals (Lai et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about a limitation supported by citations

claim: Recent data curation efforts have started to deliberately include more female individuals.
source: Recent data curation efforts have therefore started to deliberately include more female individuals (Di Martino et al., 2017; Bedford et al., 2020).
evidence: Statement about recent efforts supported by citations

claim: Cortico-cerebellar functional connectivity has repeatedly been shown to be altered in individuals with ASD, and these FC alterations have been linked to symptom severity.
source: Cortico-cerebellar functional connectivity has repeatedly been shown to be altered in individuals with ASD, and these FC alterations have been linked to symptom severity.
evidence: Statement about previous findings in the literature

claim: In the subsample with complete cerebellar coverage, FC subtypes with very similar spatial topography to the main findings were identified, suggesting that the results would not have changed substantially because of the inclusion of the cerebellum.
source: In this subsample, we identified FC subtypes with very similar spatial topography to our main findings, suggesting that our results would not have changed substantially because of the inclusion of the cerebebellum.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from the supplemental cerebellar analysis

claim: The distribution of age among individuals in the discovery and replication sample was different, despite identical sampling criteria.

claim: Individuals were excluded from the analysis if fewer than 50 time frames remained after motion censoring or if the average framewise displacement exceeded 0.3 mm.
source: Individuals were also excluded from the analysis if fewer than 50 time frames remained after motion censoring or if the average framewise displacement exceeded 0.3 mm.

source: For our main analysis we included all individuals and chose to remove all cerebellar networks.

claim: The seed based FC maps were estimated as the Pearson correlation between the average time series signal of a seed network and the time series of all gray matter voxels in the brain (excluding the cerebellum).
source: The seed to voxel FC maps were estimated as the Pearson correlation between the average time series signal of a seed network and the time series of all gray matter voxels in the brain (excluding the cerebellum).

claim: Within each sample separately, the individual seed FC maps were centered to the mean of the whole sample (ASD and NTC) and known sources of variance of non-interest were regressed for each voxel at the group level: linear effects of age, head motion and imaging site.
source: Within each sample separately, the individual seed FC maps were centered to the mean of the whole sample (ASD and NTC) and known sources of variance of non-interest were regressed for each voxel at the group level: linear effects of age, head motion and imaging site.

claim: The dissimilarity between pairs of individual seed FC maps was expressed as the absolute value of 1 minus their spatial correlation.
source: We expressed the dissimilarity between pairs of individual seed FC maps as the absolute value of 1 - their spatial correlation.

claim: FC subtypes were identified by hierarchical agglomerative clustering of the dissimilarity matrix for each seed network using the unweighted average distance linkage criterion.
source: For each seed network separately, we characterized communities of individuals with similar seed FC maps by hierarchical agglomerative clustering of the dissimilarity matrix for each seed network using the unweighted average distance linkage criterion (Müllner, 2011).

claim: Two criteria were applied for the identification of seed FC communities: (1) the average dissimilarity between seed FC maps in a community could not be greater than 1, and (2) the community had to have at least 20 members.
